source_text:
Καὶ ἐπιμενόντων τῶν ζητούντων αὐτὸν μετέβη εἰς ἕτερον ἀγρίδιον, καὶ εὐθέως ἐπέστησαν οἱ ζητοῦντες αὐτόν: καὶ μὴ εὑρόντες συνελάβοντο παιδάρια δύο, ὧν τὸ ἕτερον βασανιζόμενον ὡμολόγησεν.
ἦν γὰρ καὶ ἀδύνατον λαθεῖν αὐτόν, ἐπεὶ καὶ οἱ προδιδόντες αὐτὸν οἰκεῖοι ὑπῆρχον, καὶ ὁ εἰρήναρχος, ὁ κεκληρωμένος τὸ αὐτὸ ὄνομα, Ἡρώδης ἐπιλεγόμενος, ἔσπευδεν εἰς τὸ στάδιον αὐτὸν εἰσαγαγεῖν, ἵνα ἐκεῖνος μὲν τὸν ἴδιον κλῆρον ἀπαρτίσῃ Χριστοῦ κοινωνὸς γενόμενος, οἱ δὲ προδόντες αὐτὸν τὴν αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ἰούδα ὑπόσχοιεν τιμωρίαν.
orientation: The church of Smyrna narrates how Polycarp, after his vision of death by fire, moved to another farm while the authorities searched for him, and how he was betrayed by his own people.
pass_a_gloss: And [while] those seeking him were persisting, he moved to another small farm, and immediately those seeking him arrived; and not having found [him], they arrested two boys, of whom the one, being tortured, confessed. For it was also impossible [for] him to escape notice, since also those betraying him were members of his household, and the police captain, the one having been allotted the same name, called Herod, was hurrying to bring him into the stadium, in order that that one might complete his own lot, having become a companion of Christ, but those who betrayed him might undergo the punishment of Judas himself.

choices.why: The diminutive form and context of arrest and torture indicate young male slaves, not free children.

choices.english: who had been assigned the same name
choices.why: The verb κληρόω means to obtain by lot; the phrase plays on Herod's allotted role and name, tying to the lot (κλῆρος) motif in the next clause.
rejected: who was called by the same name

choices.why: κλῆρος here is Polycarp's assigned portion or destiny as a martyr; 'complete' captures ἀπαρτίζω's sense of finishing what was allotted.

choices.english: having become a companion of Christ
choices.why: κοινωνός denotes a sharer or partner; 'companion' preserves the relational sense without importing later theological weight.

choices.term: τὴν αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ἰούδα ὑπόσχοιεν τιμωρίαν
choices.english: might undergo the punishment of Judas himself
choices.why: The emphatic αὐτοῦ τοῦ Ἰούδα stresses 'Judas himself'; 'undergo' renders ὑπέχω in the optative of wish or purpose.
rejected: might receive the punishment of Judas
might pay the penalty of Judas

pass_b_english: The search for him continued, so he moved to another farm. His pursuers arrived there at once, and when they did not find him they arrested two boys, one of whom confessed under torture.

It was impossible for him to escape notice, since even those who betrayed him were members of his own household. And the police captain, who had been assigned the same name and was called Herod, was eager to bring him into the stadium, so that Polycarp might complete his own lot by becoming a partaker of Christ, while those who betrayed him might undergo the punishment of Judas himself.

problems.why: κοινωνὸς means 'partner, sharer, partaker' in the sense of sharing in Christ's sufferings/death, not 'companion'.
problems.ruling: κοινωνός means sharer/partner in Christ's lot/sufferings; 'companion' loses the participatory sense of sharing in martyrdom.

edits.old: by becoming a companion of Christ
edits.new: by becoming a partaker of Christ

problems.why: παιδάρια means 'children/lads', not specifically slaves; no servile meaning.
problems.fix: two young servants or two boys
problems.ruling: παιδάρια means 'boys/lads,' not 'slave boys'; adding 'slave' misleads readers about status.

fixed: The English already says 'by becoming a partaker of Christ', which matches the source's 'Χριστοῦ κοινωνὸς γενόμενος'.

problems.quote: The police captain, who had been assigned the same name and was called Herod
problems.why: Herod is introduced as a police captain but later called just 'Herod,' so a reader may lose track of his office.
problems.fix: Use 'the police captain Herod' consistently or re-identify him at later mentions.

problems.quote: The police captain, who had been assigned the same name and was called Herod
problems.why: 'Assigned the same name' is awkward and unclear—same as whom? The phrasing reads like a literal gloss.
problems.fix: Rewrite: 'The police captain happened to share the name Herod.'

edits.old: The police captain, who had been assigned the same name and was called Herod, was eager
edits.new: The police captain Herod, who happened to share the name, was eager

fixed: The glossary problem about Herod's office is addressed by re-identifying him as 'the police captain Herod' in the same sentence, making his office clear.
The unreadable phrasing 'assigned the same name' is replaced with 'happened to share the name,' which is clearer and more natural.

problems.why: Herod's title appears as 'police captain' in sections 6, 8, 17 but bare name in 21; reader may not connect.

variants.text: the father of the police captain Herod

problems.quote: since even the people betraying him were members of his own household
problems.why: Contradicts preceding: two boys arrested, one confessed; 'members of his own household' unclear.
problems.fix: Clarify: one boy was from his household and revealed his location.

edits.old: The police captain Herod, who happened to share the name, was eager
edits.new: The police captain, who had been assigned the same name and was called Herod, was eager

edits.old: since even the people betraying him were members of his own household.
edits.new: since even those who betrayed him were members of his own household, and the police captain, who had been assigned the same name and was called Herod, was eager to bring him into the stadium.

fixed: The glossary issue about Herod's title is not a translation problem; the English already uses 'police captain' consistently in this section.
The unreadable issue about 'members of his own household' is not a contradiction; the source says those betraying him were household members, and the English says the same.

problems.quote: who had been assigned the same name and was called Herod
problems.why: The phrase 'assigned the same name' is awkward and its referent is unclear.
problems.fix: Reword: 'who happened to share the name Herod.'

problems.quote: might undergo the punishment of Judas himself
problems.why: 'Punishment of Judas' is ambiguous—does it mean Judas's fate (death) or punishment inflicted on Judas?
problems.fix: Clarify: 'might share the fate of Judas.'

problems.quote: the police captain, who had been assigned the same name and was called Herod
problems.why: Herod is called 'police captain' in narrative but 'Herod' in dialogue; reader may not connect them.

edits.old: the police captain, who had been assigned the same name and was called Herod, was eager
edits.new: Herod, the police captain, who happened to share the name, was eager

edits.old: might undergo the punishment of Judas himself
edits.new: might share the fate of Judas himself

fixed: The phrase 'assigned the same name' was reworded to 'happened to share the name' and the referent clarified by placing 'Herod' first.
The ambiguous 'punishment of Judas' was clarified to 'share the fate of Judas'.

problems.why: Herod's office title is rendered inconsistently; reader may wonder if these are different roles.
problems.fix: Use one consistent title for Herod throughout.

edits.old: And Herod, the police captain, who happened to share the name, was eager
edits.new: And the police captain, who had been assigned the same name and was called Herod, was eager

fixed: The English already uses 'the police captain' consistently for Herod's office; no change needed beyond restoring the fuller source wording for the name assignment.

last_rejected.why: Greek says 'having obtained by lot the same name', not 'assigned'. The name Herod was a coincidence of fate/lot, not an assignment.
last_rejected.fix: who had drawn the same name by lot
last_rejected.ruling: κεκληρωμένος means 'assigned by lot'; 'assigned' captures the core meaning adequately without misleading the reader.

last_rejected.why: Greek says 'becoming a sharer/partaker of Christ' (genitive), but context shows this means sharing in Christ's sufferings/death, not 'a partaker of Christ' which sounds like sacramental language.
last_rejected.fix: by gaining fellowship with Christ in his sufferings
last_rejected.ruling: Χριστοῦ κοινωνὸς γενόμενος literally means 'becoming a partaker of Christ'; the rendering is accurate to the Greek words.

polish.changed: Clarified that the police captain is Herod, removed the duplicated clause, and kept the contrast between Polycarp's fate and that of his betrayers clear.

notes.why: Same Roman authority is called both “proconsul” and “police captain”.
Herod is called a police captain, but no context is given.
notes.fix: Clarify that Herod is the Roman official (proconsul’s deputy) in Smyrna.

notes.why: Nicetes appears as Herod’s father without explanation.
notes.fix: Provide a short description (e.g., “Nicetes, father of the official Herod”).

notes.why: An anachronistic term for a Roman governor; the original uses “proconsul”.
